Chapter 00 · Foundations

Start here: your first working version

Goal: In about 30 minutes, create a small, stable place for business money, business words, and business people. Not a perfect system. A working one.

Education, not legal or tax advice. This chapter mentions business structure and records only as organization topics. For decisions about how your business should be formed, taxed, insured, or contracted, use a licensed attorney or CPA, or start with the free advising described in Free help in Indiana & the US.

The 5 things every tiny business needs first

  1. A business-only email address. Not your personal inbox with a label. Something like hello@yourdomain.com later, or a separate free Gmail/Outlook account now.
  2. A business-only money trail. A separate bank account or account you use only for the business. Business banking can have fees; ask about free accounts before applying.
  3. A books home. For most US beginners, Wave Starter is the least expensive path because core accounting and invoicing are free.
  4. A way to be paid. A simple invoice with clear terms, plus a payment method whose fees you understand.
  5. A way to be found or contacted. At minimum, a one-page website and a form or email address. You don't need a brand refresh first.

Everything else is an upgrade to those five.

The 30-minute start

Minutes 0–8: Make a clean drawer

  • Create a business-only email.
  • Create three folders in a cloud drive: Clients & customers, Money, Brand & admin.
  • Inside Money, create 2026 and a monthly folder. Put receipts there.
  • Write one sentence describing what the business does and who it helps. Keep it in a note. This is your reusable introduction.

Minutes 8–20: Give the money a home

  • Open Wave and create a free Starter account.
  • Add your business name and basic details.
  • Connect the business bank account if you're comfortable doing so. If you're not ready, start with manual entries and add the connection later.
  • Do not enter years of old transactions. Start from today, or from the beginning of the current tax year after asking a professional what you actually need.

Minutes 20–30: Make the first request and first record

  • Create one invoice template.
  • Create one contact for a real or example client.
  • Write down your payment terms: when payment is due, how to pay, and where to ask questions.
  • Put a recurring 30-minute "Money date" on your calendar for the same day each month.

That is enough for day one.

What to do before forming or changing an LLC

The guide is about free tools, not entity selection. But since LLC questions come up early, here are organization guardrails—not recommendations about whether or not to form an entity:

  • Indiana filings start with INBiz. It is Indiana's official business filing portal: https://inbiz.in.gov/. Avoid cold calls and look-alike "LLC filing" sites that charge a service fee for something you can file directly. Confirm any fee shown in INBiz before paying.
  • An EIN is free from the IRS. Apply directly at https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/apply-for-an-employer-identification-number-ein-online. Never pay a third party just to "get an EIN" unless they're providing a service you understand and want.
  • An LLC is not a free pass on taxes or paperwork. Annual reports, registered agent/office requirements, local licenses, taxes, and insurance can still apply. Ask the SBDC or a professional what applies to your situation.
  • Don't sign a template because it's free. Free legal templates can be useful starting points, but a lease, business contract, operating agreement, or employment document may need an Indiana attorney's review. See Legal-template resources.
  • Don't use a home address without thinking. Public filings may expose an address. Registered-agent options and privacy trade-offs vary. Ask a professional or the Secretary of State.

Do not add a second tool in a category until the first one actually hurts. Free tools are only cheap if you use them.

Set up a backup rhythm now

Software is rented. Your records are yours.

  • Monthly: export your accounting data as CSV and a PDF report. Download invoices.
  • Monthly: export contacts or copy the CRM data somewhere you control.
  • Monthly: download a copy of your email list (where the plan allows) and keep it in your private files.
  • Quarterly: download your website source or repository and confirm you can restore it.
  • Quarterly: check current free-plan limits and renewal dates.
  • Whenever you change tools: export before you cancel.

Keep the backup in a private folder with access limited to you. Don't post exports to public repositories or AI chats.

AI helper: your "set up the boring parts" prompt

Use a free chatbot, but redact personal and financial details first. Never paste account numbers, EINs, customer data, or documents you don't own.

You are a calm operations assistant for a one-person business. Ask me
five short questions about how money, customers, and documents currently
flow through my business. Then give me a 7-step setup plan that takes no
more than 30 minutes per step. Keep the tools free, avoid asking me for
sensitive information, and label every guess as [assumption]. End with a
one-page monthly maintenance checklist. This is organizational help, not
legal, tax, or financial advice.

Then verify every recommendation against the tool's official pricing page.

Chapter 01 · Money

Accounting: know the numbers without becoming an accountant

The job: Keep a clean, understandable record of money that came in, money that went out, and what still belongs to whom. You are not trying to produce a tax return by yourself. You are trying to avoid a shoebox in April.

Not tax, accounting, or financial advice. Expense treatment, estimated taxes, payroll, sales tax, inventory, home offices, and multi-state issues are fact-specific. Use a CPA or enrolled agent for decisions. Free tools help you organize; they don't replace professional review.

The free starting point: Wave Starter

Wave offers a free Starter plan in the US and Canada that includes core accounting and unlimited invoicing. Paid add-ons and card processing exist; you do not need them to start bookkeeping.

Why it's the recommendation for a very small US business:

  • It's one place for income, expenses, and invoices.
  • It works on a phone and in a browser.
  • The free plan is usable rather than a short trial.
  • It can connect to a bank account, which reduces manual entry.

Alternative for a non-US business: Wave's availability varies. Check local free options and local accounting requirements. Do not pretend a US tool handles another country's tax rules.

Alternative for a spreadsheet lover: A simple spreadsheet is honest and infinitely exportable. It is not the best choice if you will forget to update it or need bank connections. If you use a spreadsheet, log every transaction, keep receipts, reconcile monthly, and export a copy.

What "good bookkeeping" actually looks like

At minimum, every transaction should answer:

  1. Date — when it happened.
  2. Description — what it was.
  3. Amount — how much.
  4. Account/category — what kind of money it was.
  5. Receipt or evidence — a document that supports it.
  6. Business purpose — a short note for anything unclear.

For a one-person business, a monthly rhythm matters more than a fancy chart of accounts. A clean modest set of categories beats 87 micro-categories you can't explain.

Set up Wave in about 45 minutes

  1. Create the free account. Choose the Starter plan. Dismiss paid add-ons unless you already know you need them.
  2. Add the business details. Legal name, address, currency, and logo if you have one. Use your business email.
  3. Connect the business account. Read the permissions screen. Wave uses a third-party connection provider; understand what it can see. If you're not ready, skip the connection and add transactions manually this week.
  4. Set a simple chart of accounts. Start with broad buckets such as sales, contract income, software, supplies, advertising, transaction fees, professional services, and owner draws/contributions. If you're unsure, leave something labeled "Ask my accountant" rather than guessing.
  5. Import only the current year. Don't recreate six years of history unless a professional says to. Duplicate transactions create duplicate problems.
  6. Categorize 10 transactions. Learn where the review screen lives. Don't aim for perfection; aim for a repeatable monthly pass.
  7. Attach your first receipts. Save a PDF or image to your Money/2026 folder. Receipt scanning may be a paid add-on; a phone photo plus a consistent folder is still useful.
  8. Create a customer and one invoice. You can learn invoicing in the next chapter.
  9. Label owner money correctly. If you take money out of the business, don't call it a mysterious expense. Ask a professional how owner draws/contributions should be recorded for your tax classification.
  10. Export a test copy. If you can't find the export screen, you're not ready to trust the tool. Make notes.

The 25-minute monthly money date

Put it on the calendar. Bring a drink. Do the same steps in the same order.

Step 1 — Reconcile (8 min). Match the bank transactions in Wave to reality. Investigate duplicates and missing transactions. The goal is that Wave agrees with the bank.

Step 2 — Categorize and annotate (8 min). Clear the review queue. For anything ambiguous, write a question instead of inventing an answer. Save it on a running "ask my accountant" list.

Step 3 — Check invoices (4 min). Look at unpaid invoices and send a friendly reminder. Record any payment fees. Don't count money as received until it's actually received.

Step 4 — Close the month (3 min). Export a CSV of transactions and a simple profit-and-loss report. Download any new invoices and receipts into the monthly folder. Write a one-line summary: "October: two invoices paid, one late, $X in business software."

Step 5 — Make one decision (2 min). Choose one small improvement for next month: ask for a deposit, raise a price, cancel an unused tool, or book help.

A note about receipts

Sophisticated receipt scanning is convenient, but not required on day one. What matters:

  • Save receipts the same week.
  • Name files with date, vendor, and amount.
  • Keep them in a private folder with backups.
  • Match receipts to the transaction list.
  • Ask a professional how long to keep records for your situation.

Wave's receipt-scanning feature may require a paid add-on. Check the current pricing page. Also check whether a mobile photo stored in your own folder is enough for your workflow; don't pay for scanning just to create the same result.

Free-plan watch-outs

  • Card payments and bank connections are not the same as accounting. Payment processing fees are separate from the free bookkeeping plan.
  • Wave's "free" can include upsells. The account is free; payroll, payments, receipts, or other modules may cost money. You can say no.
  • No tax filing included. Wave may offer tax products in some regions, but you remain responsible for filing. A free tool is not a tax preparer.
  • Data export matters. Test the export now, not during an emergency.
  • Don't mix personal and business spending if you can avoid it. A clean account saves hours. Ask your bank about fee-free business options.
  • AI can organize; it cannot sign off. Never ask a chatbot to determine your tax deduction without verifying with a professional.

AI helper: the monthly close buddy

Use a free AI assistant only after removing names, account numbers, and other sensitive details.

Act as a careful bookkeeping assistant, not a CPA. I will paste
anonymized descriptions of this month's transactions. Sort them into my
existing categories, list anything ambiguous as a question rather than a
guess, and create a 20-minute month-end checklist. Do not advise me on
tax deductions, filing positions, or whether an expense is deductible.
Do not invent amounts or vendors. End with three questions to ask my
accountant.

Good uses of AI here: explain a confusing report in plain English, draft a checklist, summarize a month you describe, generate a list of questions.

Bad uses: paste raw bank statements, ask it to file taxes, ask it to decide if something is deductible, trust its math without checking.

Chapter 02 · Money

Invoicing: ask for money clearly, then follow up kindly

The job: Send a professional request for payment with unambiguous terms, make paying easy, and follow up without waiting three months and developing a stomachache.

Not legal or tax advice. Contract terms, late fees, deposits, sales tax, and what happens when a client doesn't pay depend on your agreements and jurisdiction. Templates and scripts in this guide are educational starting points. For a high-value or disputed invoice, talk to an attorney or CPA.

The free starting point

Best all-free standalone: Zoho Invoice

Zoho Invoice is free for what most one-person businesses need, with limits as of this writing: up to two users, three projects, and 500 invoices per year. It produces professional invoices, estimates, and payment links. It may display "Powered by Zoho" branding. Payment gateway fees are separate.

Best if you already use Wave: Wave invoices

If you set up Wave Starter for bookkeeping, use its invoicing instead of adding a second system. Fewer places for revenue to get lost. Wave's accounting and invoicing are free on Starter, with paid processing and optional add-ons.

Pick one home for invoices. Do not invoice from Wave for one client, Zoho for another, and a Canva PDF for a third. That is how records become archaeology.

What a beginner-friendly invoice needs

Use plain fields and avoid legal-sounding filler you can't explain.

  • Your business name and contact information
  • Your customer's name and contact information
  • A unique invoice number and issue date
  • A clear description of what you delivered (or milestones)
  • Quantity, rate, and total
  • Any tax you're required to charge (ask a professional; don't guess)
  • Payment terms: due date, accepted methods, and who pays processing fees, if consistent with your agreement
  • Deposit or late-fee terms only if they were agreed in advance
  • A link or instructions to pay
  • A short, friendly note: what to do if something looks wrong
  • The word DRAFT until you verify it

If you're selling physical goods, include shipping and return information where applicable. If you're selling digital goods or services, make sure the scope and delivery date are clear.

Set it up without overthinking

  1. Create one branded template. Business name, logo, one accent color, readable font. No decorative clutter.
  2. Set numbering. Use a simple consistent scheme, such as 2026-001, 2026-002.
  3. Set payment terms. Common options include due on receipt, Net 7, Net 14, or Net 30. Pick what you can actually enforce and state it on the invoice. For larger projects, ask about a deposit. Your contract controls; this is not legal advice.
  4. Connect a payment method only if needed. Card payments take a percentage. Bank transfer options vary. Clearly distinguish what you receive from what the customer pays.
  5. Create a reusable follow-up schedule. Put it on your calendar: due date, +3 days, +7 days, +14 days. Friendly persistence is not rude.
  6. Test with a $1 demo invoice to yourself if the tool permits. Confirm the payment page, confirmation email, and receipt work.
  7. Download every paid invoice and save it with the matching bookkeeping record.

A simple follow-up ladder

Tone: warm, specific, and easy to act on. No passive-aggressive poems.

Before due (2–3 days early): "Hi [Name] — just a quick heads-up that invoice #2026-014 for [project] is due Friday. Here's the payment link if you need it. Thanks!"

Due date: "Hi [Name] — invoice #2026-014 is due today. I've attached a copy. If it's already scheduled, thank you—no need to reply. If something looks off, tell me and I'll take a look."

3 days late: "Hi [Name] — checking in on invoice #2026-014, now three days past due. Could you let me know the expected payment date? I'm happy to resend the link."

7–14 days late: "Hi [Name] — I still don't see payment for invoice #2026-014. Please send a payment date today, or let me know if there's a dispute so we can resolve it. If we agreed on a late fee, note it without inventing new terms."

After 14 days: pause, check your contract, and decide whether to escalate. If it's a significant amount or there's a dispute, get professional advice rather than sending a threatening template.

Good boundaries: stop additional work if your agreement allows it, keep everything in writing, and don't release final files or deliverables you aren't obligated to release. Check the actual contract—not a stranger's internet script.

Deposits, late fees, and taxes

These are contractual and tax matters. The free-tool guide cannot decide them for you. Practical guardrails:

  • Put terms in the agreement, not only on the invoice.
  • Don't invent late fees after a dispute. If you want late fees, discuss the wording with a professional and include it upfront.
  • Check sales tax. Services and products are treated differently in different places. Indiana businesses should start with the Indiana Department of Revenue and get advice for their specific offerings.
  • Use a CPA or tax pro for 1099 questions. Whether you must issue or file forms is fact-specific.
  • Keep invoices and payments consistent. If the invoice says $500 and the bank shows $487.25 after processing fees, record the fee as a fee—not as an invoice that was only partly paid.

Free-plan watch-outs

  • Zoho Invoice is not a full accounting system. Pair it with a bookkeeping workflow, or use Wave for both books and invoices. Don't assume your income is tracked just because you sent an invoice.
  • Zoho's free limits include 500 invoices/year and two users. That's generous for a beginner, but confirm current terms on the official pricing page.
  • Payment links are not free money. The payment processor charges a fee. Read the rate before enabling it.
  • Branding appears on free plans. That is usually fine. Don't pay just to remove it until the business justifies it.
  • The customer's inbox is not your filing cabinet. Download paid invoices and back them up.
  • Free plans can change. Keep the export button on speed dial.

AI helper: the follow-up draft

Never paste real customer names, bank details, or contract terms you don't own.

You are a calm, friendly billing assistant for a one-person business.
Draft a payment follow-up email for this situation: [describe timeline,
amount, and prior contact in general terms, with no personal data]. Keep
it under 110 words. Be warm, specific, and firm. Include one clear next
step and a deadline. Do not threaten legal action, invent a late fee, or
claim legal rights. Give me two versions: one for a first reminder and one
for 14 days overdue.

Use it as a draft. Put the real facts in yourself. Verify the due date and contract terms.

Chapter 03 · Customers

CRM: remember people without keeping a brain full of sticky notes

CRM stands for customer relationship management. In a tiny business, it mostly means: know who you talked to, what you promised, and what happens next. You do not need an enterprise platform to do that.

Not legal advice. Privacy, marketing consent, record retention, and data protection rules vary. Collect less personal information, protect what you collect, and ask a qualified professional when a customer relationship involves sensitive or regulated data.

The free starting point

Simple and free forever: a spreadsheet

For your first 20–50 relationships, a spreadsheet can be the right CRM. Use columns such as:

  • Name
  • Preferred name and pronouns (optional, for respectful communication)
  • Email / preferred contact method
  • How they found you
  • What they're interested in
  • Last conversation date
  • What I promised
  • What they promised
  • Next action and due date
  • Consent / source of contact
  • Notes (no sensitive data)

This is boring, exportable, and easy to understand. The weakness is that it needs manual updating and doesn't remind you by itself.

When you need a pipeline: HubSpot Free

HubSpot's free CRM stores up to 1,000 contacts for free, with no time limit, and includes core contact and deal management. It is a good next step when you have more conversations than your memory can carry or you want reminders, pipelines, and a shared view of customer activity.

Why it can be a good beginner choice:

  • Free contact and deal management.
  • A real interface for follow-ups rather than an infinite spreadsheet.
  • You can start with no paid onboarding.
  • It can grow with you if the business someday needs more.

Why it is not automatically the answer:

  • It's a large product with many upsells. A tiny business can get lost in modules it doesn't need.
  • Free-plan limits and features change.
  • It stores customer data in a third-party cloud. You need a reason, permission, and a security habit.
  • HubSpot's broader marketing and sales products can become expensive. The free CRM does not mean the whole platform is free.

Start with the simplest tool that makes you follow through. If a spreadsheet works, don't install a CRM to feel professional.

Build a one-person pipeline that stays small

You need fewer stages than the internet suggests. Try four:

  1. New — someone made contact.
  2. Talking — a real conversation is happening.
  3. Proposal / next step — you've offered something or agreed on a next action.
  4. Won or lost — with a one-line reason.

Then add a next action and due date to every open contact. A pipeline with no next actions is a museum.

The 15-minute weekly relationship review

Once a week, open the CRM (or spreadsheet) and do this:

  • Which conversations have no next action? Add one.
  • Who is waiting on me? Send the thing.
  • Who am I waiting on? Send one gentle nudge.
  • Who is a good fit for what I offer now? Send a useful, non-spammy note.
  • Update "won/lost" so the pipeline reflects reality.
  • Archive the people who asked not to be contacted.

Get consent right, keep data minimal

These are practical guardrails, not legal advice:

  • Record where the contact came from. "Bought a list" is not a good starting point for permission-based outreach.
  • Don't buy email lists. They damage deliverability and create consent problems.
  • Make unsubscribing or asking not to be contacted easy. Honor requests promptly.
  • Don't collect sensitive data just because you have a notes field. No Social Security numbers, health diagnoses, passwords, or bank credentials.
  • Respect health privacy especially. If you work with healthcare audiences, do not place patient information in an ordinary CRM. HIPAA and related obligations are specialized; get professional guidance.
  • Limit access. Enable two-factor authentication. Don't share a login on a sticky note.
  • Export quarterly. A contact list you can't export is not fully yours.

Set up HubSpot Free without drowning

  1. Create an account with your business email.
  2. Explore Contacts and Deals only. Ignore other navigation for now.
  3. Create a four-stage pipeline: New, Talking, Next step, Won/Lost.
  4. Add five real contacts that you have permission to store. Skip sensitive notes.
  5. Add a next action and due date for each open contact.
  6. Connect your business email only if you understand what data the tool will access.
  7. Create a recurring 15-minute weekly review.
  8. Test export and data deletion before you rely on it.

If the idea of setting up a "pipeline" makes you sigh, use the spreadsheet. Seriously. A functioning low-tech system beats an abandoned high-tech one.

Free-plan watch-outs

  • "Free CRM" does not mean free marketing automation. Check the boundaries before uploading your list.
  • Contact limits count contacts, not just customers. Know what happens at the cap and whether duplicates count.
  • Email tracking has privacy implications. Recipients and regulators may care about tracking pixels and consent. Don't enable every tracking feature by reflex.
  • The CRM is not your email marketing platform. Keep sales conversations and consented newsletters in the appropriate tool.
  • No free plan owes you indefinite storage. Back up.
  • Do not treat AI-generated summaries as facts. A confident summary can still be wrong. Check the record.

AI helper: turn notes into a follow-up plan

You are a careful relationship assistant. Turn these meeting notes into a
CRM record using only facts I provide: [paste redacted notes]. Output:
1) two-sentence summary, 2) what I promised, 3) what they promised,
4) one next action with a suggested date, 5) one short, warm follow-up
email. Mark anything missing as TBD. Do not invent names, amounts, or
commitments. Do not make legal, tax, or medical recommendations.

Good uses: organize notes, draft a follow-up, prepare for a call, suggest a polite nudge.

Bad uses: store customer secrets in a free chatbot, infer sensitive traits, automate cold outreach, or let it write promises you haven't approved.

Chapter 04 · Customers

Email marketing: stay in touch without becoming a spammer

The job: Send useful, expected emails to people who asked to hear from you; make unsubscribing easy; keep your list portable. An email list is a borrowed audience, not a guaranteed sales funnel.

Not legal advice. Marketing-email rules depend on where you and your recipients are. In the US, the FTC's CAN-SPAM guidance is a useful official starting point. If you sell to the EU/UK or handle regulated information, get jurisdiction-specific advice. Never put health records or sensitive personal data in a marketing tool.

The free starting point

Best for a small permission-based list: MailerLite Free

MailerLite currently offers a free plan with up to 250 subscribers and 2,500 monthly emails, plus two user seats. That's a real starting point for a one-person business, but small. You'll outgrow it before you get famous.

Good fit:

  • You want a proper signup form, consent record, and unsubscribe handling.
  • You have a growing but small list.
  • You want campaign and automation features without a monthly bill.
  • You can live within the subscriber and monthly-send limits.

More daily sends: Brevo Free

Brevo currently offers a free plan with 300 emails per day, a drag-and-drop editor, templates, automation, and A/B testing. Free plans and send allowances change; check the official page for current contact and daily limits before moving a list.

Good fit:

  • You send small batches frequently.
  • You want to explore a combined email/CRM platform.
  • You can stay under a daily sending ceiling.

Don't run both for the same list. Pick one. Duplicates, unsubscribes, and double sends are how trust gets lost.

The one thing that matters most: permission

A list is not a number. It's a set of people who expect your mail. Build it with:

  • Explicit signups from your website, a form, a workshop, or a direct request.
  • Clear expectations: what you'll send and how often.
  • Double opt-in if your tool supports it. It asks people to confirm by email and reduces typos and bad addresses.
  • A real unsubscribe link. Do not hide it.
  • An honest physical mailing address in commercial email, as required in the US. Use a business mailing address you control; don't use someone else's home without permission. Check the FTC guidance and your tool's help docs.
  • A relationship, not a purchased file. Buying lists is a fast route to spam complaints and deliverability problems.

If someone says "stop emailing me," honor it. Don't re-add them because they downloaded a new lead magnet. Keep a do-not-contact record.

Set up a small email system

  1. Choose one home. Do the free-plan math for the next six months, not just today.
  2. Create a signup form. Ask for the minimum: usually an email address and, optionally, a first name. Explain what they'll get.
  3. Set the consent language. Keep a dated record of where and when each contact signed up. A checkbox or active opt-in is clearer than a prechecked box.
  4. Write a welcome email. It should arrive immediately, confirm what they signed up for, set expectations, and offer one useful next step.
  5. Make one helpful monthly email. A practical tip, a link roundup, an update on your book or services, or a question. Not five calls to action.
  6. Add a plain-text unsubscribe line. Your provider handles the mechanism; don't bury it.
  7. Test it. Send to yourself and a friend. Check mobile, links, images with alt text, footer address, and unsubscribe.
  8. Authenticate your domain when you own one. Set up the records your provider recommends (often SPF, DKIM, and DMARC). This is a deliverability practice, not legal advice. Use the provider's current setup guide.
  9. Export your list quarterly. You should know what leaving looks like.

A calm first-month rhythm

  • Week 1: Welcome email + one useful resource.
  • Week 2: Short note about who you help and one thing you're working on.
  • Week 3: Practical tip or a question you've been getting.
  • Week 4: Review: opens are a weak signal but still a signal. What did people reply to? What caused unsubscribes? Adjust.

Metrics to watch without obsessing: delivery, replies, clicks, unsubscribes, and complaints. Open rates are distorted by privacy features and image blocking. A small list with replies is healthier than a giant list that never responds.

CAN-SPAM guardrails in plain English

The FTC guidance describes requirements including accurate header information, truthful subject lines, clear identification of commercial messages where required, a physical postal address, and a working opt-out mechanism that is honored promptly. There are also rules about third-party sending. Read the official guide; this is not legal advice.

Also avoid:

  • Fake "Re:" or "Fwd:" subject lines.
  • Manufactured deadlines and invented scarcity.
  • Health, financial, or earnings claims you cannot support.
  • Sending to people who didn't ask.
  • Putting customer information or health data in the email content without a proper legal basis.

Free-plan watch-outs

  • Subscriber counts include more than customers. Bounced contacts and unsubscribed contacts may count differently. Check the tool.
  • Monthly sends are not the same as unlimited emails. A big launch can hit a limit mid-month.
  • Automation features and support vary by plan. Confirm before designing a workflow.
  • Free-plan branding may be added. Usually acceptable; pay only when the brand cost is real.
  • Cheap does not mean compliant. You remain responsible for consent and accurate claims.
  • Deliverability is not guaranteed because you use a free tool. A warmed domain and relevant content matter.

AI helper: build a welcome sequence that sounds human

Help me draft a four-email welcome sequence for [describe audience]
who signed up for [lead magnet or reason]. Use plain English and short
paragraphs. No fake scarcity, no income claims, no health claims. Each
email must be under 180 words and contain one clear call to action.
Output for each: subject line, preview text, body, and one fact or link
I need to verify before sending. End with a checklist for consent,
unsubscribe, and a physical mailing address. This is marketing help,
not legal advice.

Then do the human part: cut the hype, verify every claim, check the footer, and send it to yourself first.

Chapter 05 · Be found

Website & hosting: a small home on the internet

The job: Give people one trustworthy place to understand what you do, contact you, and buy only if you actually need to sell online. A small static site is enough for most authors, consultants, freelancers, and service businesses getting started.

Not legal advice. Privacy policies, accessibility obligations, advertising claims, and e-commerce requirements depend on your business and audience. Get help when you collect data, sell regulated products, or make claims about outcomes. Never put API keys or other secrets in a public website.

Two free hosts, two different jobs

GitHub Pages

GitHub Pages hosts static sites directly from a GitHub repository, free. It supports custom domains and HTTPS.

Use it when:

  • You're comfortable with a repository or willing to learn.
  • Your site is informational: an author hub, documentation, a project page, a portfolio.
  • You don't need server-side form handling, logins, or e-commerce.
  • You're okay with the repository being public on GitHub Free. Publishing a Pages site from a private repository requires a paid GitHub plan; check current docs.

Official limits and rules to know:

  • Repositories and published sites have a 1 GB recommended maximum.
  • Bandwidth has a soft 100 GB/month limit and builds a soft 10/hour limit.
  • GitHub says GitHub Pages is not intended or allowed as free hosting to run your online business, e-commerce site, or any other site primarily directed at commercial transactions or providing commercial SaaS. Don't use it for a storefront. Read the current official limits page before choosing it.
  • Don't collect sensitive data through a GitHub Pages site.

For a free informational author page or open-source project, GitHub Pages is an excellent fit. For a business site whose main purpose is commercial transactions, choose a host whose terms allow that.

Netlify Free

Netlify is a static hosting platform with drag-and-drop or Git-based deploys, HTTPS, custom domains, deploy previews, and more backend features.

Use it when:

  • You want to drag a folder of files into a browser and get a live site.
  • You want easier custom domain and deploy-preview workflows.
  • You're building a commercial brochure site or need optional form/functions features.
  • You want to experiment without running a server.

Current free-plan reality (checked October 22, 2026): The free plan shows a 300-credit monthly limit covering usage such as production deploys, compute, form submissions, bandwidth, and requests. Different actions consume credits. A small static site should fit comfortably, but AI/function features or viral traffic can use more. Netlify's 2024 free-plan announcement described commercial projects as allowed; terms and credit mechanics have evolved, so confirm current pricing and terms before relying on that for a business-critical site.

Honest comparison

GitHub PagesNetlify Free
Setup styleGit repository, GitHub Actions or branchDrag-and-drop or Git
Custom domain + HTTPSYesYes
Best forDocs, portfolios, informational pages, open sourceSmall business brochure sites, previews, forms
Form handlingNo built-in backendSome form/function options within plan limits
Commercial / storefrontNot allowed as primary commercial hostFollow current terms; static brochure use is common
Main catchPublic repo on GitHub Free; commercial-use languageUsage credits and changing plan terms

A domain is not free. A custom .com usually costs roughly $10–$25 per year, sometimes less for the first year and more on renewal. A *.github.io or *.netlify.app subdomain is free. Start there if money is tight. Buy a domain when it helps people remember and trust you.

Build the smallest useful site

Five pages or fewer:

  1. Home — who you help, what you offer, one next step.
  2. About — a credible short bio, no fake credentials.
  3. Work / books / services — what you actually offer, with real details.
  4. Contact — email or a form, plus expectations for response time.
  5. Privacy & disclosures — what data you collect, if any; affiliate and advertising disclosures where applicable.

For an author: add a book page, a simple email signup, and a clear way to request a talk or workshop. For a service business: add scope, starting price or a clear "request a quote," and a booking link. For a reseller: follow the marketplace rules and host only content you own.

Write like a person

  • Lead with the customer's problem, not your origin story.
  • Use short headings and real examples.
  • Put contact details where people expect.
  • Tell people what happens after they contact you.
  • Use real testimonials only with permission. Never invent reviews or results.
  • Add alt text to meaningful images; leave decorative images with empty alt.
  • Check color contrast and keyboard navigation.

Publish without leaking secrets

  1. Start locally. Build or write the files in a private folder.
  2. Check for secrets. Search for API_KEY, SECRET, passwords, personal addresses, unredacted client files, and analytics tokens you don't recognize. Never commit .env files.
  3. Use a public repository only for public content. GitHub history is not a secret vault.
  4. Deploy via Netlify Drop or a Git integration. Follow the host's current steps; don't guess an old workflow.
  5. Set the custom domain and HTTPS. Follow DNS instructions exactly. Changes can take time to propagate.
  6. Test on a phone and with a keyboard. Open every link. Check the contact route. Check the 404 page.
  7. Add a privacy note if you collect anything, even an email address through a form.
  8. Keep an offline copy. Download the repository or a ZIP of the published files. Your host is not your backup.

Forms, analytics, and privacy

  • Static hosts don't automatically give you a database. Use a free form tool such as Tally or Google Forms, or a host's form product, and review where submissions go.
  • Don't collect SSNs, payment details, health information, or passwords through a generic form.
  • If you add analytics, choose a privacy-respecting option, disclose it, and avoid collecting more than you need. Many free analytics tools use cookies; if you're subject to GDPR/UK GDPR, get proper advice on consent.
  • Keep site JavaScript minimal. Never expose an API key in client-side code. If a tool needs a secret, it needs a server or a trusted integration.

Free-plan watch-outs

  • Free hosting can have soft limits. A popular post can create a bandwidth bill or site suspension if limits are exceeded.
  • Terms matter more than "it says free." GitHub Pages is explicitly not a free e-commerce platform.
  • A custom domain is a recurring cost. Don't forget the renewal.
  • Email on your domain may be a separate paid service. A domain does not automatically include a mailbox.
  • Free SSL certificates still require configuration. Follow the host's instructions.
  • Don't host a community or customer portal on a static site. Static means no secure login or private data storage.

AI helper: edit the homepage without adding fiction

Review this homepage copy for clarity, warmth, and accessibility: [paste
copy with no customer data]. The audience is [describe]. Rewrite it at a
plain-English reading level. Do not invent testimonials, credentials,
statistics, or outcomes. Keep a maximum of one primary call to action.
Flag any claim that needs evidence. Suggest heading structure and alt-text
ideas for images I describe. This is editing help, not legal advice.

AI is useful for tightening copy and drafting a privacy page outline—not for making up reviews or promising legal compliance. Check the final content yourself.

Chapter 06 · Be found

Design: look put-together without a design degree

The job: Make your business recognizable and readable across invoices, your website, social posts, and simple documents. Clarity is the design goal. Polish is a bonus.

Not legal advice. Image licences, font licences, trademarks, and advertising rules matter. Use assets you have permission to use, don't copy another brand's distinctive identity, and verify licensing before publishing or selling merchandise.

The free starting point: Canva Free

Canva Free is the easiest free design tool for a beginner. As of October 22, 2026, the free plan includes 5 GB of cloud storage and up to 20 uses of Standard or Premium AI tools, plus millions of free templates and assets. Premium elements are watermarked or require payment; you cannot just export them legally for free.

Good first uses:

  • A simple logo lockup (your name in a chosen typeface, not a fake crest).
  • One invoice header and one letterhead.
  • A website hero graphic or open-graph card.
  • Social profile images and a reusable announcement template.
  • A one-page service or book sell sheet.
  • A simple brand sheet for yourself.

Understand the licensing

Canva's free content is generally available for commercial and noncommercial use under its content licence, but premium content is different, logos and brands can have extra restrictions, and licence terms can change. Read the current Canva licensing explanation and Content License Agreement yourself.

Practical rules:

  • Filter for free elements.
  • Don't use a watermarked preview in a live project.
  • Don't use Canva's stock or templates in a way the licence forbids (for example, some standalone asset resale uses).
  • Don't upload someone else's copyrighted character, logo, or photo.
  • Keep source links for any external asset you use.
  • If you sell physical products with a design, check the licence for print-on-demand and merchandise.

Build a tiny brand kit

You do not need a rebrand. You need consistency. Create a one-page note with:

  • Name and short description. How the name is capitalized.
  • One primary color. A deep green, navy, oxblood, or plain black. Dark text on light backgrounds is easiest.
  • One accent color. Use it for links, buttons, and highlights—not every sentence.
  • Two typefaces at most. One for headings, one for body. System fonts (Georgia, Palatino, Arial, Segoe UI) are free and render everywhere. If using web fonts, check the licence, load locally where possible, and don't depend on an external service for a privacy-first site.
  • One look for images. Photos with the same warmth and light quality, or simple line illustrations. Avoid a collage of unrelated stock.
  • A clear voice. Warm, direct, plain English; no fake urgency.
  • Contact details. Business email, website, and city/state if appropriate. Don't put a private home address on public graphics.

Starter palette recipe

Use a contrast checker before you publish. For normal text, aim for at least the WCAG AA contrast ratios (4.5:1 for small text; 3:1 for large text). Dark brown-green #17342B on warm cream #F8F1E3 is an example of a high-contrast pairing. A bright orange on cream might look nice and still fail—check, don't vibe.

Make the five assets you actually need

  1. A simple wordmark: your business name set in one font, with good spacing. Skip the clip-art icon for now.
  2. A social profile image: name readable at small size. Avoid tiny taglines.
  3. A link-preview image: 1200 × 630 px usually works for sharing. Include your name and a short line.
  4. An invoice header: logo or name, email, website. Use the same header on quotes.
  5. One social/announcement template: duplicate it, change the text, keep the layout.

Then stop. A brand is not a 60-page PDF. It's recognition plus trust.

Design rules that make a beginner look experienced

  • Hierarchy: one big headline, one supporting line, one call to action. If everything is loud, nothing is.
  • Whitespace: let things breathe. Margins are not wasted space.
  • Alignment: pick a left edge and stick to it. Canva's alignment guides are your friend.
  • Contrast: dark text on light backgrounds, or light text on genuinely dark backgrounds. Don't use yellow text on white.
  • Small text: don't go below sensible body sizes (roughly 16px on the web). On print, no 5-point footnotes.
  • Images: one strong image beats five decorative ones. Provide alt text on the web.
  • Consistency: same colors, same two fonts, same logo placement.
  • Restraint with AI images: don't create fake people who look like your customers or fake product photos. Disclose material use where appropriate. Keep human judgment.

File organization that saves future-you

Create Brand/ with:

Brand/
  brand-sheet.md
  logo/
    wordmark-light.png
    wordmark-dark.png
    favicon.svg
  templates/
    invoice-header
    social-square
    link-preview
  licenses/
    asset-sources.md

Export PNG for everyday sharing, SVG or PDF for print-quality logos when available. Keep editable Canva links and a local exported copy. If your Canva account goes away, you should still have the assets you need.

Accessible by default

  • Use real text instead of text baked into images when possible.
  • Keep body copy at a comfortable size and line length.
  • Check contrast (a free contrast checker is enough).
  • Add captions/transcripts to video.
  • Don't rely on color alone to communicate (for example, red/green only).
  • Add alt text for informative images: describe the purpose, not every pixel.
  • Make buttons and links look clickable.
  • Test your site with the biggest text setting and keyboard-only navigation.

AI helper: make a design brief, not a logo dump

Create a one-page design brief for my small business. Ask me five short
questions about my audience, the feeling I want, references I like, and
where the design will be used. Then propose: one primary color, one accent
color, two system-font choices, five layout rules, and a list of five
assets I actually need. Do not invent a logo concept or claim the colors
pass accessibility—tell me to test contrast with a checker. Keep the tone
warm and plain.

Use AI for structure, editing, and alternatives. Don't ask it to imitate a living artist's style or reproduce a trademark.

Free-plan watch-outs

  • Premium templates and images can trap you at download. Canva Free may let you edit with premium elements but require payment or a watermarked export. Filter to free.
  • AI usage is limited on the free plan. As of this check, up to 20 uses. Don't plan a 30-asset AI campaign on it.
  • Cloud storage is not a backup. Export and back up important assets.
  • Canva is not a trademark search. A name that looks good can still infringe someone else's rights.
  • Free fonts on one site may cost money on another. Check the licence for web, print, merchandise, and embedding.

Chapter 07 · Customers

Scheduling: end the "what about Tuesday?" spiral

The job: Let people book a real meeting at a real time without exposing your whole calendar or exchanging nine emails. The best booking page is short, clear, and connected to a calendar you actually keep current.

Not legal advice. If you handle appointments for healthcare or other regulated services, don't collect clinical details in a generic booking form. Use systems and policies appropriate to your obligations. This guide covers general business scheduling only.

The free starting point

Most flexible for one person: Cal.com Free

Cal.com is an open-source-friendly scheduling platform with a free plan for one user, unlimited event types, calendar syncing, and integrations. It's a strong choice for a solo business that wants several meeting types—intro call, book-a-session, podcast interview, office hours—without paying per event type.

Why it works:

  • One-person plan with unlimited event types.
  • Connects to Google Calendar, Outlook, and other calendars.
  • Good fit for local-first/self-hosting-minded users if you later want more control.
  • White-labeling and larger teams are paid upgrades, not requirements for getting booked.

Classic simple option: Calendly Free

Calendly's free plan includes one event type, one calendar connection, and a customizable booking page as of this writing. If you offer exactly one kind of meeting—say, a 20-minute discovery call—that's enough. If you need separate 15/30/60-minute meetings, Cal.com's free plan is more flexible.

Use Google Calendar or another calendar as the source of truth. The booking tool is the doorbell; the calendar is the house.

Set up a booking page people can trust

  1. Choose one meeting type. For a first version: "Intro call — 20 minutes." Write a one-sentence purpose.
  2. Connect one calendar. Avoid connecting several personal calendars with sensitive event titles unless you understand what's shared.
  3. Set availability. Keep it honest. Don't advertise 7 a.m.–9 p.m. if you'll resent every booking.
  4. Add buffers. Five or ten minutes between meetings saves the day. Set a minimum notice period (for example, 24 hours) and a booking horizon (for example, the next 30 days).
  5. Check time zones. Enable time-zone display. Confirm what the confirmation email shows. Don't book anyone at 3 a.m. by accident.
  6. Add location. Auto-generated video link or a clearly stated phone/address. Don't put a private home address unless it's appropriate and safe.
  7. Write a short description. What you'll discuss, what to bring, what happens next.
  8. Set cancellation and reschedule rules. Include a link for reschedules and a gentle notice request. Let people leave without a guilt trip.
  9. Send a confirmation with a clear subject line. "Confirmed: 20-minute intro call, Tue Oct 27, 2:00 p.m. ET."
  10. Test it yourself. Book a slot, check the calendar event, click the video link, cancel, and reschedule.

Keep it humane for you and them

  • Batch calls when you can. Two or three call slots on certain days is easier than calls scattered through every day.
  • Protect focus time. Mark unavailable blocks in your calendar. Good boundaries prevent bad meetings.
  • Add a pre-meeting form only when it helps. A required form can create friction. Ask only what you need.
  • Don't put intake questions in the event description if they contain sensitive info. Use a secure form and disclose retention.
  • Have a no-show lane. Send one friendly note: "I missed you today. Want to find another time?" Then move on.
  • Accessibility: send a link, not just a phone number; use captions when available; offer a contact method for adjustments.
  • Consent: no adding attendees to your newsletter just because they booked a call.

A tiny scheduling toolkit

Event type: Intro call (20 min)
Purpose: Understand the project and decide the next step
Location: Video link generated by the tool
Availability: Tue/Thu, 10:00–14:00 local, with 10-minute buffers
Notice: 24 hours minimum
Reschedule: allowed up to 12 hours before
Who brings what: a short description and the one decision you want to make

Write this in a note and reuse it. Don't reinvent your meeting policy every week.

Free-plan watch-outs

  • Cal.com's free plan is for one user. Team routing and advanced branding are paid.
  • Calendly's free plan is one event type. Multiple meeting types or advanced workflows can require a paid plan.
  • The scheduling tool is not your calendar. If you don't maintain the calendar, you'll double-book.
  • Video conferencing may have its own limits. Google Meet, Zoom, and Microsoft Teams free options change. Check current host and participant limits.
  • Booking data lives in a third party. Read the privacy terms and don't collect health details unnecessarily.
  • "Unlimited event types" doesn't mean unlimited everything. Integrations, workflows, or branding may still have limits.

AI helper: write a booking invitation that respects everyone's time

Draft a short booking email for [a specific type of meeting]. My booking
page is [describe, not paste a private link]. Offer two relevant time
windows in [time zone], include a 45-minute reschedule option, and state
that the meeting is [length]. Ask for one piece of context in advance.
Keep it under 100 words and warm, not salesy. Do not claim anyone else's
availability unless I give it to you.

Use AI for wording, not for inventing available times. The calendar knows the truth.

Chapter 08 · Customers

Forms: ask less, get better answers

The job: Collect the information you need for a quote request, intake, feedback survey, or application—without becoming a data hoarder. A good form is short, accessible, and clear about where the answers go.

Not legal or tax advice. Privacy, consent, data-retention, healthcare, children's data, and payment-card rules are specialized. When in doubt, collect less and get professional guidance. Never ask for Social Security numbers, passwords, full card numbers, or medical details through a generic form.

The free starting point

Tally Free

Tally offers unlimited forms and submissions on its free plan, with features such as logic, integrations, and payments, and Tally branding. It's a clean, beginner-friendly form builder and often the best fit for a small business that needs a professional-looking intake form for free.

  • Free file uploads: individual files up to 10 MB on the free plan as of this writing. Check current storage and submission terms.
  • Perks: conditional logic, answers in a spreadsheet-like view, integrations, and a simple editor.
  • Catch: free-plan branding, and advanced features or higher limits may require a paid plan.

Google Forms Free

Google Forms is free with a Google account. It's basic, familiar, and stores responses in Google Sheets or Drive. It's a good choice if you already live in Google Workspace-adjacent tools and need a simple questionnaire.

  • Strengths: quick setup, spreadsheet responses, simple sharing.
  • Weaknesses: less control over advanced logic and design; data lives in a third-party ecosystem; account security matters.
  • Watch: consumer Gmail accounts and business accounts have different data/administration implications. Don't put sensitive records in a personal form.
  • Storage limits: Google's help documentation lists a 1 GB total storage limit and a 500,000 responses per form limit for Forms starting September 2026. File uploads can consume that storage quickly. Check the current limit before using Forms as a file-intake system.

Pick one. Don't collect the same answers in two forms and then manage two incompatible spreadsheets.

What belongs in a beginner form

Use exact, neutral labels. Make the required minimum obvious. Examples:

For a quote request

  • Name and preferred contact method
  • Email
  • What do you need help with? (long answer)
  • Desired deadline and budget range (optional, if appropriate)
  • How did you find me?
  • Consent checkbox: "OK to contact me about this request."

For a workshop interest list

  • Name (optional)
  • Email
  • One question you want answered
  • Consent checkbox with a link to how you'll use the email

For feedback

  • One rating, one open question, and one optional contact field
  • Thank-you page with next steps

Do not ask for a birthdate, home address, income, diagnosis, or ID number unless there is a specific, legitimate business reason and a safe system. A form is not a secure vault.

Build a form that gets completed

  1. Write the decision first. "What will I do with this response?" If there's no action, remove the question.
  2. Name the form in plain language. "Project request" beats "Inquiry Intake v3."
  3. Use one page for a short form. Long forms need sections; short forms need respect.
  4. Use clear field labels. Labels above fields, not placeholder-only text that disappears.
  5. Mark optional fields as optional. Don't make everything required.
  6. Add help text for confusing questions. "Budget range helps me scope this" is friendlier than an unlabelled dropdown.
  7. Explain privacy. Where will responses go? Who sees them? How long will you keep them?
  8. Add a confirmation message. Tell people what happens next and when to expect a reply.
  9. Test accessibility. Keyboard navigation, visible focus, error messages, and sufficient contrast.
  10. Test the notification and export. Submit a fake entry, receive the email, find the row, export a CSV.

Data hygiene for one-person businesses

  • Use a business account with two-factor authentication.
  • Limit access. Don't share the admin login.
  • Review responses on a schedule. Turn off collection when the campaign ends.
  • Export and archive what you need for your records, then consider deleting unnecessary form submissions.
  • Don't use a form for e-signatures. A typed "I agree" field in a general form isn't a complete signing workflow. Use a dedicated e-signature tool and get legal advice for important agreements.
  • Avoid healthcare data. If you educate healthcare workers, keep educational feedback separate from patient information. Never collect PHI through a free form.
  • Be careful with file uploads. Accept only the formats you need, set size expectations, and never allow executable files.
  • Watch third-party integrations. Every connected app is another place data can leak.
  • Spam happens. Add a simple challenge or accept that you'll delete junk. Don't collect extra personal data just to "verify everyone."

Free-plan watch-outs

  • "Unlimited submissions" does not mean unlimited uploads or features. File sizes, storage, and advanced capabilities vary.
  • Free branding appears. That can be a trust signal for a small business, not an emergency.
  • Personal Google accounts lack business-grade admin controls. Fine for low-risk; not for sensitive data.
  • Deleting a form may not immediately delete every response copy. Check the help docs and maintain your own retention plan.
  • Third-party form tools process data on your behalf. Read the privacy policy if you collect customer data.

AI helper: turn a messy list of questions into a decent short form

I need a form for [purpose]. Here are my rough questions: [list]. Rewrite
them as clear, accessible labels, remove anything that is not necessary
for this purpose, and mark optional fields. Flag any request for sensitive
personal data and suggest a safer alternative. Produce a short consent
sentence, a confirmation message, and a one-page internal data-retention
note. Do not claim that this makes me compliant with any privacy law.

Then delete at least one question. That's not an AI instruction; it's a form-design rule.

Chapter 09 · Paperwork

E-signature: get simple documents signed without paper

The job: Send a document for signature, keep a record of who signed and when, and save the completed copy where you can find it. Electronic signatures are ordinary business practice, but the tool is not a lawyer.

This chapter is not legal advice. Whether an electronic signature is enforceable, what notices are required, and which documents can be signed electronically depend on the document, the parties, and the law. Federal ESIGN and Indiana's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act generally recognize electronic signatures, but there are important exceptions and practical proof requirements. Ask a licensed attorney for anything consequential. Never use a generic tool for wills, court filings, or documents where a professional has told you not to.

The free starting point: DocuSeal

DocuSeal is an open-source e-signature platform. Its hosted free plan is small—currently 10 emailed documents per month, with unlimited templates—and it also offers a self-hosted option via the open-source project. For a one-person business that signs a few simple client agreements a month, the free plan can be genuinely useful.

Why it's a good fit:

  • Simple templates and signing fields.
  • An audit trail and completed PDF.
  • Open-source code available for self-hosting if you have the technical ability.
  • No need to pay for basic signing on day one.

Why self-hosting is not "free" for everyone:

  • You need to run and secure a server.
  • You own patches, backups, uptime, and access control.
  • Misconfigured self-hosted software can expose private contracts.
  • Email deliverability and SMS verification may require extra services.
  • Self-hosting is a technical project, not a beginner requirement.

If you don't need an online workflow yet, a PDF emailed with clear instructions and a returned signed copy can work for some low-risk documents. That doesn't remove the need for an appropriate agreement or proof; ask a professional when signatures must meet a specific standard.

What an e-signature is—and isn't

An electronic signature is a way to show intent to sign a record electronically. It is not just a typed name in a contact form. A useful workflow records:

  • The document that was presented
  • The signer's identity/email and intent
  • The time and date
  • Consent to do business electronically, where appropriate
  • The final signed document plus an audit certificate
  • A copy provided to each signer
  • A retention plan for your business records

The tool helps with the mechanics. The agreement and the circumstances determine enforceability. This guide can't tell you whether a particular document qualifies. For significant agreements, use an attorney.

Set up a small signing workflow

  1. Decide if this document should be signed online. Wills, certain family/court documents, and some notices may be excluded or need specific formalities. Ask a lawyer if you're unsure.
  2. Use a document you have the right to use. Don't upload someone else's contract without permission.
  3. Create a template only for repeatable, low-risk documents. Examples: a simple client agreement your attorney has reviewed, a speaking release, or a basic author-services schedule.
  4. Add fields deliberately. Signature, date, initials, name, and maybe an agreed checkbox. Don't ask for extra sensitive information.
  5. Set signing order. Who signs first? Does the other party sign after you?
  6. Write a plain-language email. Identify the document, why it's being sent, and who to ask with questions. Don't pressure anyone to sign immediately.
  7. Test with your own email. Sign a dummy document. Check the final PDF, audit trail, and confirmation messages.
  8. Save the completed document. Put it in a private folder with a date and descriptive name. Back it up. DocuSeal is not your permanent records system.
  9. Give each signer a copy. Keep the final PDF and any certificate. Don't rely solely on a dashboard link.
  10. Delete or archive drafts according to your retention plan. If a document contains personal information, limit who can access it.

Signature caution checklist

  • Is this document consequential enough that a professional should draft or review it? If yes, stop.
  • Are all pages present, legible, and the correct version?
  • Do the names, dates, addresses, and payment terms match reality?
  • Is each signer authorized to sign for their side?
  • Is the signature placement correct?
  • Does the signer receive a completed copy?
  • Does the audit trail identify the signer and timestamp?
  • Have you stored it privately and backed it up?
  • Have you avoided collecting ID numbers or health data that you don't need?
  • Would you be comfortable explaining the process in a dispute? If not, get advice.

Free-plan watch-outs

  • 10 documents/month is a real ceiling. Count envelopes, not pages. Check what DocuSeal counts before sending a batch.
  • Branding and advanced features may be limited. That's okay for a small operation.
  • Self-hosting transfers responsibility to you. Include server, backup, security, and maintenance costs in the decision.
  • Free tools do not provide legal review. A signature does not make a bad agreement good.
  • Completed signatures contain personal data. Don't put them in public GitHub repos, unencrypted shared drives, or AI chats.
  • SMS verification may cost extra or be unavailable. Confirm the workflow you need.

AI helper: understand before you sign—or ask better questions

Explain this contract excerpt in plain English, sentence by sentence:
[paste an excerpt you own, redacting names and sensitive details]. List
the deadlines, payment terms, cancellation/termination terms, deliverables,
and anything ambiguous. Then give me 8 questions to ask the other party or
an Indiana business attorney. Do not tell me whether the contract is
enforceable, whether to sign it, or what the law requires. Do not draft a
new contract. This is for my understanding only.

AI can help you notice words. It cannot take responsibility for a legal decision.

Chapter 10 · Paperwork

Legal-template resources: start with official forms, not random PDFs

The job: Find trustworthy starting points for routine filings and documents, know what a template cannot do, and prepare better questions for a licensed professional.

This chapter is education, not legal advice and not a substitute for an attorney. Filing a form or using a template does not create a lawyer-client relationship. Contract, employment, privacy, tax, and entity questions depend on specific facts. The sources below are official or established starting points, but you must verify that a form is current and appropriate for your situation.

A hierarchy of trust

Use documents in this order, and only when you understand what you're filing:

  1. Official government forms and portals for filings the government actually requires.
  2. Official guidance that explains the filing process, deadlines, and common mistakes.
  3. Reputable educational templates from SBA resource partners, clearly labeled as generic.
  4. Templates from commercial providers—read the licence, terms, state-specific disclaimers, and marketing claims carefully.
  5. A document a licensed attorney drafted or reviewed for your situation, when the stakes justify it.

A random PDF with a professional-looking header is at the bottom of that hierarchy. Free does not mean accurate or state-specific.

The core official resources

1. Indiana formation, reports, and entity records

  • INBiz is Indiana's official business filing portal: https://inbiz.in.gov/.
  • Use it to form an entity, file entity reports, update information, and search business records.
  • The Indiana Secretary of State's business resources are at https://www.in.gov/sos/business/.
  • Indiana requires entities to maintain a registered agent and registered office in the state. Confirm current requirements in official guidance and ask a professional if you're unsure how privacy, virtual agents, or commercial registered agents interact with your situation.
  • Don't pay an unfamiliar third-party "LLC filing service" from a cold call before checking INBiz and understanding what the service actually adds.

Important: Filing formation documents is not the same as having a complete operating agreement, licenses, permits, tax registrations, insurance, or good contracts. You may not need all of those immediately, but "I formed an LLC" is not a full legal foundation.

2. Federal tax and identification forms

  • EIN online: free and official at https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/apply-for-an-employer-identification-number-ein-online.
  • Form W-9: official PDF and instructions at https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-w-9. You provide a W-9 to a requester who needs your taxpayer identification number; this page says not to send the form to the IRS.
  • Small business and self-employed center: https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed.
  • Schedule C: https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-schedule-c-form-1040.
  • Self-employed tax center: https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/self-employed-individuals-tax-center.
  • Publication 334, Tax Guide for Small Business: https://www.irs.gov/publications/p334.

Ask a CPA or enrolled agent which forms and elections apply to you. An LLC is not a tax classification by itself. Do not let an AI or a template decide your tax status.

3. Indiana tax and employer registrations

  • Indiana Department of Revenue, business taxes: https://www.in.gov/dor/i-am-a/business-corp/.
  • INTIME (Indiana Taxpayer Information Management Engine) is linked from DOR guidance for business tax filing.
  • If you hire anyone, there may be state registration, withholding, unemployment insurance, and workers' compensation questions. Do not copy an employment package from the internet. Use official guidance and a professional.

4. Free business templates and education

  • SCORE resource library: https://www.score.org/resources/. SCORE offers free business mentoring and a library of articles, templates, and tools. Templates are generic—check dates, assumptions, state-specific issues, and whether the licence allows your use.
  • SBA Business Guide: https://www.sba.gov/counseling/#business-guide. Start here for business planning, launch, management, and funding basics.
  • SBA local assistance: https://www.sba.gov/counseling/local-assistance/. SBA resource partners can provide free or low-cost counseling, but they do not replace your lawyer or CPA.
  • Indiana SBDC: https://isbdc.org/. No-cost advising and training, including business planning and referrals.

Template map for a tiny business

NeedA reasonable starting pointWhat a template can't do

EINIRS EIN applicationChoose your tax classification or answer state registration questions
Record customer TINIRS W-9 formDecide whether you need one or what to do with it

No legal decision by checklist. Use this map to know what to search for and what to ask, not as a green light.

An operating agreement, specifically

An operating agreement is generally an internal document that describes how an LLC is run and how owners relate to it. The rules and practices around them vary, and the document isn't a generic form you can assume is right. Ask an Indiana business attorney:

  • Do I need an operating agreement for my situation?
  • What should it say about ownership, capital, distributions, decision-making, deadlocks, transfer, and dissolution?
  • Does it need to be filed or kept internal?
  • How should it interact with my tax elections and estate plan?
  • What happens if I'm a single-member LLC?

Free templates can be a place to collect questions, not a final answer. This guide doesn't tell you whether you need one.

How to vet any free template

  • Who published it? Government? Bar association? Established nonprofit? Named law firm? Anonymous SEO site?
  • When was it updated? A 2014 template can be worse than no template.
  • Is it state-specific? Generic wording may conflict with Indiana rules.
  • What licence applies? Can you use it commercially? Can you modify it? Are there attribution requirements?
  • What does it leave out? Templates rarely know your scope, risks, compliance duties, or negotiation.
  • Is the layout hiding traps? Check all pages, footnotes, and cross-references.
  • Does it contain placeholders you don't understand? Don't sign or send it until you do.
  • Does it ask for sensitive data you shouldn't collect? Limit data and secure storage.
  • Would you be comfortable reading it aloud to the other person? If not, get help.

What to bring to an attorney

  • A one-page description of the business and the decision you're making.
  • The draft document, clearly marked up with your questions.
  • Names of the parties, relationship context, and timeline.
  • Your budget and desired outcome.
  • Relevant emails or prior agreements, redacted as appropriate for secure transmission.
  • A list of questions ranked from "must understand" to "nice to know."

Not every legal problem needs a full engagement. Some attorneys offer short consultations, flat-fee reviews, or unbundled document review. Ask about cost and scope upfront. Your local bar association can help you find an appropriate lawyer. Free business advising from SCORE or the SBDC can help you prepare, but they are not your lawyer.

AI helper: prepare for a legal conversation

I am preparing questions for a licensed Indiana business attorney about
[describe the document or decision, without sensitive personal details].
My business is [one sentence]. I do not want you to draft a legal document
or tell me what the law is. Produce: 1) a one-page context summary I can
review, 2) eight specific questions to ask, 3) the documents I should
bring, 4) five terms I should ask them to explain in plain English, and
5) the facts I should verify before the meeting. Remind me to redact
sensitive information before sharing anything.

AI is a preparation aid. The attorney provides advice based on your facts and the actual law.

Chapter 11 · Learn & get help

Free training & templates: learn the skill, not just collect the certificate

The job: Build the specific skills your business actually needs—bookkeeping basics, marketing, a little web work, AI literacy—without buying a $499 course you never finish. Templates are part of the same job: they give you a decent starting point so you can spend your energy on the parts that are uniquely yours.

This is education, not legal, tax, or financial advice. A course, certificate, or template does not make you a lawyer, accountant, or licensed professional. Training quality and free offers change. Check the provider's official page before you invest time. Never pay an unsolicited "training" provider that guarantees income or government approvals.

The learning rule that saves the most time

Learn one skill that removes a current bottleneck, practice it on your real business, then stop.

Collecting courses feels productive. Applying one lesson to a real invoice, a real webpage, or a real customer email is what changes the business. A 45-minute session with a blank page beats a 40-hour video library you bookmark and avoid.

Free training worth knowing

Government and nonprofit training

  • SBA Learning Platform — free, self-paced courses on starting, planning, marketing, finance, and managing a business: https://learning.sba.gov/.
  • SCORE — free mentoring plus free webinars, courses, and a large resource library: https://www.score.org/ and https://www.score.org/resources/.
  • Indiana SBDC — no-cost one-on-one advising and training for Indiana businesses: https://isbdc.org/.
  • IRS Small Business and Self-Employed Tax Center — official guides, forms, and recordkeeping basics: https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed.
  • FTC Business Guidance — plain-language consumer-protection and advertising rules: https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance.
  • DigitalLearn — free, beginner-friendly computer and internet basics from the Public Library Association: https://www.digitallearn.org/.
  • Your local public library — many libraries offer free access to online course platforms, research databases, and in-person tech help. Ask your branch what your card includes; offerings vary.

Free vendor academies worth the time

These are run by companies that sell software. That does not make them useless—it means you should expect product-focused lessons and upsells.

Templates are not strategy. A business plan template with optimistic numbers is still optimistic. A contract template that doesn't match your scope is still a contract. Use templates to organize thinking, not to replace it.

A four-week learning plan you can actually finish

One 45-minute session per week. Pick a real task, not a certificate.

Week 1 — Money literacy (45 min). Watch one SBA or SCORE session on cash flow. Then open your own numbers and write down three questions. Book a free SBDC or SCORE appointment to ask them.

Week 2 — Marketing that fits you (45 min). Take one HubSpot Academy or Google Skillshop lesson. Write one useful email or one service page using what you learned. Publish it.

Week 3 — Your website or design (45 min). Use one Canva Design School lesson to fix one real asset: homepage header, invoice header, or social profile. Export it and use it.

Week 4 — AI with boundaries (45 min). Read AI helpers and set up one assistant for low-risk drafting. Write your redaction rules. Test one prompt on a real, non-sensitive task.

At the end, write one sentence: "I learned ___ and used it to ___." If you can't fill in the second blank, the course was entertainment, not training.

How to vet free training

  • Who made it? Official agency, established nonprofit, recognized company, or anonymous funnel?
  • When was it updated? Tax, platform, and marketing advice goes stale quickly.
  • Is there a real exercise? Watching is not the same as doing.
  • What is the upsell? A free lesson that ends in a $2,000 coaching pitch is an advertisement, not a course.
  • Does it promise income or approvals? "Guaranteed" is a warning sign, not a feature.
  • Does the certificate mean anything? Usually it documents attendance, not professional licensure. Don't put a vendor certificate in a bio as if it were a degree or credential.
  • Is your data safe? Don't upload customer records, health information, or financial account numbers to an unknown learning platform.
  • Can you use the template commercially? Read the licence. "Free" often means personal use only.

Chapter 12 · Learn & get help

Free help in Indiana & the US: real people, no sales pitch

The job: Know where to get qualified, free or low-cost guidance before you guess, overpay, or fall for a scam. The best free resource is not a PDF—it's a person who has seen your situation before and will tell you what to do next.

This chapter is education, not legal, tax, or financial advice. Free advisors can explain programs and offer general guidance; they are not your attorney, CPA, or financial advisor, and they cannot guarantee a loan, grant, contract, or approval. Verify eligibility and deadlines with the official agency. Never pay an unsolicited caller who says they can "unlock" a government grant.

Who to contact first

For most Indiana one-person businesses, the shortest path is:

  1. Indiana SBDC for no-cost business advising and a local point of contact: https://isbdc.org/.
  2. SCORE for a free mentor and free workshops, especially if you want a long-term sounding board: https://www.score.org/.
  3. SBA local assistance to find the resource partner that fits your situation: https://www.sba.gov/counseling/local-assistance/.
  4. The official agency for filings, taxes, and licenses—INBiz, the Indiana Department of Revenue, or the IRS. Free advice does not replace an official filing.

Free does not mean low quality. SCORE volunteers are often retired executives. SBDC advisors work with small businesses every day. Come prepared and you will get more than a generic brochure.
