A note on "free" advising: SCORE and SBDC advising are designed to be no-cost, but always ask before a meeting whether any service has a fee. Legitimate organizations do not demand a payment to "hold" your free appointment or "activate" a grant.

What free help can and cannot do

A good advisor can:

  • Explain how a program, form, or process works in plain English.
  • Review your plan or numbers and point out gaps.
  • Help you prepare questions for an attorney, CPA, or lender.
  • Connect you with local programs, workshops, and peers.
  • Tell you when a paid professional is genuinely worth it.

An advisor cannot:

  • Give you legal advice or sign off on your contract.
  • Prepare or sign your tax return.
  • Approve a loan, grant, or government contract.
  • Guarantee that a business idea will work.
  • Make a decision that is yours to make.

If someone offers a guarantee, treats a free service as a sales funnel, or asks for sensitive information before you have verified who they are, stop and verify through the official website.

How to get real value from a 30-minute appointment

Before the meeting, write a one-page brief:

  • What the business does, in one sentence.
  • Who it serves and how it makes money.
  • The specific decision or bottleneck you need help with.
  • What you have already tried.
  • The three questions you most need answered.
  • Your timeline and rough budget.

Bring or have ready: your business name and entity type, your website or draft, a simple revenue/expense picture, and any relevant document with sensitive details redacted. Do not send your Social Security number, EIN, bank credentials, or customer health information by ordinary email.

During the meeting:

  • Ask, "What would you do next if this were your business?"
  • Ask, "What am I not asking that I should be?"
  • Write down the advice and the source.
  • Ask whether they can refer you to a specialist.

After the meeting: send a two-line thank-you that summarizes the next step. Put the follow-up on your calendar.

A short outreach email

Subject: Request for a free advising session — [business name]

Hi [organization],

I'm the owner of [business name], a [one-sentence description] in
[city], Indiana. I'm working on [specific decision or problem] and would
like a 30-minute advising session.

Current situation: [2–3 sentences, no sensitive data].
What I've tried: [1–2 sentences].
My three questions:
1. [question]
2. [question]
3. [question]

I'm available [two time windows]. I understand this is general business
guidance, not legal or tax advice. Thank you.

[Name]
[Business website or phone]

Keep it under 200 words. A clear, specific request gets a faster reply than "I want to start a business, please advise."

Scam protection, in plain English

Government resources are free to access. Anyone charging you to "apply for an EIN," "file your LLC," or "claim a free grant" is selling a service or running a scam.

Red flags:

  • An unsolicited call, text, or DM saying you qualify for a "free government grant."
  • A fee before you can see the grant, loan, or program details.
  • A website that looks like the SBA or INBiz but has a different URL.
  • Pressure to pay today, or a "deadline" that disappears tomorrow.
  • A request for your SSN, EIN, bank login, or a copy of your ID before you have verified the organization.
  • A "mentor" who guarantees approvals, asks you to buy gift cards, or moves the conversation to a private messaging app.
  • Paid "certification" or "registration" that is not required by any agency.

Safer habits:

  • Type the official address yourself: sba.gov, irs.gov, inbiz.in.gov, in.gov.
  • Search the organization's name plus "scam" before paying anyone.
  • Use a separate business email and a password manager.
  • Ask an advisor you met through the SBDC or SCORE to review an offer before you sign.
  • Report suspected fraud at https://reportfraud.ftc.gov/ and, for internet crime, https://www.ic3.gov/.

Specialized free help

  • Veterans and military spouses: SBA Veterans Business Outreach Centers.
  • Women entrepreneurs: SBA Women's Business Centers.
  • Minority-owned businesses: MBDA Business Centers.
  • Government contracting: APEX Accelerators.
  • Exporting: SBA and the U.S. Commercial Service offer counseling and market information; start with the SBA local assistance page.
  • Agriculture, childcare, and other regulated sectors: ask the SBDC for the agency that governs your industry before relying on general advice.

Eligibility rules vary. A center that is not the right fit will usually refer you; that is still a useful call.

AI helper: prepare for a free advising session

I have a free 30-minute advising appointment with [SCORE / Indiana SBDC /
SBA resource partner]. My business is [one sentence]. The decision I need
help with is [describe, without sensitive data]. Produce: 1) a one-page
brief I can read aloud, 2) eight specific questions ranked by importance,
3) the documents I should bring, 4) three things I should not share in an
email, and 5) a follow-up note template. Do not give legal, tax, or
financial advice. Do not invent program names or eligibility rules.

Use the output to prepare. Confirm every program detail with the official agency.

Chapter 13 · AI, carefully

AI helpers: drafts, not decisions

The job: Use free AI to get unstuck on drafting, summarizing, planning, and explaining—without handing it your secrets, your judgment, or your legal and tax decisions. AI is a fast intern with no memory of your business and a habit of sounding certain when it is wrong.

This is education, not legal, tax, accounting, or medical advice. AI output can be inaccurate, outdated, biased, or invented. Verify facts, numbers, links, prices, and policy details against official sources. Never use AI to diagnose or treat a patient, give medical advice, or replace a licensed professional. Never put protected health information, client data, account numbers, EINs, passwords, or API keys into a chat you do not control.

Start with the right kind of AI

For a one-person business, "AI" usually means one of three things:

KindWhat it isGood first useMain caution
Hosted chatbotA website or app that runs a model for youDrafting, summarizing, explaining, brainstormingYour input leaves your device; check data controls
Local AIA model running on your own computerPrivate drafting and organizingHardware limits; still verify output
Coding assistantAI inside an editor or terminalLearning code, fixing small errorsReview every change; never expose secrets

Pick one hosted assistant and learn it well. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Perplexity all offer free tiers, but limits and terms change. The best free assistant is the one whose privacy settings you understand and whose answers you actually check.

Set up privacy before you get productive

Do this once, before you paste anything real.

  1. Use a business-only account. Do not mix a personal account full of family photos and banking emails with your business drafts.
  2. Find the data controls. Look for settings about model training, chat history, and "improve the service." Turn off training or data improvement where the provider offers it. Terms differ; read the current policy.
  3. Use temporary or incognito chats for one-off questions when available.
  4. Assume anything you paste could be stored. The safest sensitive document is one you never upload.
  5. Redact before you paste. Replace names with [CLIENT], amounts with [AMOUNT], addresses with [CITY], and account numbers with [REDACTED].
  6. Turn on two-factor authentication for the account.
  7. Keep a simple rule: no SSNs, EINs, bank logins, passwords, API keys, medical records, contracts you don't own, or other people's private information.

Free consumer plans are not a secure records system. If you need a signed business agreement, use document storage, not a chat history.

A redaction checklist

Before pasting, scan for:

  • Names, email addresses, phone numbers, and home addresses
  • Social Security numbers, EINs, tax IDs, and dates of birth
  • Bank and card numbers, routing numbers, and account balances
  • Passwords, recovery codes, API keys, and access tokens
  • Patient information, diagnoses, prescriptions, and insurance IDs
  • Unpublished book text, client materials, or someone else's contract
  • Anything you would not want a stranger to read

If removing the detail makes the prompt useless, the task probably needs a local tool or a human professional—not a public chatbot.

Local AI: free, private, and a little nerdy

Local tools run a model on your own computer. Nothing is sent to a cloud service, which is appealing for sensitive drafts. The trade-off is hardware, setup, electricity, and model quality.

Worth knowing:

  • Ollama — a beginner-friendly way to run models locally.
  • LM Studio — a desktop app with a chat interface and model downloads.
  • llama.cpp — the lower-level engine many local tools build on.
  • Open WebUI — a self-hosted chat interface for local or hosted models.

A practical minimum is a reasonably recent computer with 16 GB of RAM for small models; larger models need more. A small local model can organize notes and draft routine text. It is not automatically safer to trust—it can still hallucinate. It is safer with data, not necessarily with facts.

Do not self-host on the public internet just to "have AI." If you expose a chat interface without authentication, you may expose your files. Local means local.

Free AI coding helpers

If you want to learn to build a small tool or fix your own website, these are legitimate starting points. Free plans and limits change constantly.

  • GitHub Copilot Free — AI suggestions inside common editors for eligible GitHub accounts: https://github.com/features/copilot.
  • Gemini CLI — an open-source command-line assistant with a free tier for Google accounts: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli.
  • Cline — an open-source coding agent for VS Code; you provide the model: https://cline.bot/.
  • Continue — open-source AI assistance you can configure with local or hosted models: https://continue.dev/.
  • Aider — open-source pair programming in the terminal; model usage may cost money: https://aider.chat/.
  • OpenRouter — one API for many models, with some free models and usage limits: https://openrouter.ai/.

Coding safety rules:

  • Never paste API keys into a chat or commit them to a repository.
  • Review every code change before running it. AI can introduce security bugs.
  • Don't give an agent broad access to your email, bank, or file system until you understand its permissions.
  • Test on a copy before changing a live site.
  • Keep backups and version control.

Agents and MCP tools can be genuinely useful, but they can also take actions. A beginner should start with read-only suggestions, not an autonomous agent with your passwords.

Prompt patterns that work for a tiny business

JobPrompt shapeVerify
Setup plan"Ask me five questions, then give a 7-step plan under 30 minutes per step"Tool limits and prices
Invoice reminder"Warm, under 110 words, one clear next step, no invented late fee"Due date and contract terms
CRM notes"Summarize only the facts I provide; mark missing facts TBD"Names and commitments
Welcome email"Four short emails, no fake scarcity, one CTA each"Claims and footer address
Homepage copy"Plain English, one primary CTA, no invented testimonials"Every factual claim
Design brief"Propose colors, system fonts, and five assets; tell me to test contrast"Accessibility contrast
Form cleanup"Remove unnecessary questions; flag sensitive data"Data you actually need
Contract questions"Explain this excerpt and list questions for an attorney"A licensed attorney
Learning plan"45-minute practice-first session with a self-check"Official course details
Monthly close"Sort anonymized transactions; list ambiguous items as questions"Your accountant

A reusable business helper prompt

Save this as a starting point. Change the role and constraints, not the privacy rules.

You are a calm, practical assistant for a one-person business. Use plain
English and short paragraphs. Ask before assuming. Label every assumption
as [assumption]. Do not invent facts, prices, laws, links, testimonials,
or statistics. If you are unsure, say so and tell me what to verify.
Never ask me for passwords, account numbers, EINs, health information, or
other sensitive data. Do not give legal, tax, medical, or financial
advice; instead, list questions for a licensed professional. Keep outputs
short enough to use today.

Then add the task. The constraints do a lot of work.

The verification checklist

Before you use any AI output:

  • Facts: Can you find the claim on an official or primary source?
  • Numbers: Did you recalculate totals and dates yourself?
  • Links: Does the link load, and is it the official page?
  • Law and tax: Did a licensed professional confirm the rule for your situation?
  • Health: Is this education only, with no patient-specific advice?
  • Privacy: Did you remove names, IDs, and sensitive details?
  • Tone: Does it sound like you, or like a generic brochure?
  • Responsibility: Are you willing to stand behind the final version?

If the answer to the last question is no, don't send it.

What AI should not decide

  • Whether an expense is deductible, or how to classify your LLC for tax.
  • Whether a contract is enforceable or safe to sign.
  • Whether a patient should receive a treatment or a diagnosis.
  • Whether a marketing claim is legal or substantiated.
  • Whether a person is trustworthy, hirable, or creditworthy.
  • What your prices, boundaries, or values should be.

AI can help you prepare better questions for the humans who carry that responsibility.

AI helper: audit your own AI use

Audit my AI workflow as a cautious operations assistant. I will describe
the tools I use and the kinds of information I paste, without sharing
actual sensitive data. Identify: 1) places where I might be exposing
personal or business data, 2) tasks where a local model or a human
professional is a better fit, 3) three prompts I should rewrite to
include verification steps, and 4) a one-page monthly AI hygiene
checklist. Do not claim that any setup is legally compliant. Do not ask
for secrets.

Run this audit once a quarter, or whenever you add a new tool.

Chapter 14 · Put it together

The 90-day plan: one small session a week

The job: Turn this guide into a working business system without losing a weekend. One 45–60 minute session per week, one real outcome per session. If a week goes sideways, you have not failed; you have a plan with a next step.

This is education, not legal, tax, or financial advice. The plan organizes free tools and learning. It does not decide your entity, taxes, contracts, insurance, or licenses. Book a free SBDC or SCORE session early, and use a licensed professional for decisions that matter.

The rules

  1. One bottleneck at a time. Do not sign up for every tool in week one.
  2. Use real work. A real invoice, a real contact, a real page. Practice data teaches nothing.
  3. Stop at "working," not "perfect." You can polish after the business has a pulse.
  4. Export before you depend. Test the exit door while the tool is still free.
  5. If you miss a week, skip don't stack. Do the next session; don't do two in one sitting and resent the plan.

The 13-week map

WeekSessionDone whenStart here
1Clean drawerBusiness email, password manager, 2FA, three folders, one-sentence descriptionStart here
2Money homeWave (or a spreadsheet) set up, bank connected or manual entries started, 10 transactions categorizedAccounting
3First invoiceOne template, clear terms, one test invoice, payment method understoodInvoicing
4People systemSpreadsheet or HubSpot Free, five real contacts, a next action on each, 15-minute weekly review bookedCRM
5Website v1Home, About, Offer, Contact, and Privacy pages live on a free host; every link testedWebsite & hosting
6Brand kitOne-page brand sheet, wordmark, social image, link preview, invoice header, contrast checkedDesign
7Booking + formsOne booking type connected to a calendar, one short form tested end to endScheduling, Forms
8Email listSignup form, consent language, welcome email, unsubscribe tested, list exportedEmail marketing
9DocumentsOne low-risk document template, test signature, completed copy saved and backed upE-signature
10Ask for helpSBDC or SCORE appointment booked, one-page brief written, top questions listedFree help
11Learn + AI setupOne 45-minute training session applied to a real task, AI privacy settings reviewed, redaction rules writtenFree training, AI helpers
12Backup drillBooks, contacts, email list, invoices, website, and documents exported; one restore test completedStart here
13Review + rhythmCurrent free-plan limits checked, one upgrade chosen or deliberately declined, recurring maintenance sessions bookedSources & fine print

A realistic time budget: 45–60 minutes for the session, plus a few minutes during the week to gather information. Week 5 may take two sessions if you are learning hosting from scratch. That is normal.

What each session actually produces

Weeks 1–4: the foundation. By the end of week 4 you should be able to answer: Where does business email live? Where does money go? How do I ask for payment? Who am I following up with, and when? If those answers are clear, the rest is easier.

Weeks 5–8: the front door. You do not need a perfect brand. You need a page that explains what you do, a way to contact you, a way to book you, and a way to stay in touch with permission. Publish before you feel ready, then fix what confuses real people.

Weeks 9–12: the back office. This is where free tools earn their keep: simple signatures, free advising, one useful skill, and a backup you have actually restored. A backup you have never tested is a hope, not a backup.

Week 13: the review. Open every tool's pricing page. Compare your usage to the limit. Cancel what you don't use. Decide whether one paid tool would save more time than it costs—and write down why. "No" is a valid answer.

The maintenance rhythm after 90 days

RhythmTimeWhat happens
Weekly15 minRelationship review: next actions, waiting-on, one useful follow-up
Monthly25 minMoney date: reconcile, categorize, check invoices, export CSV and P&L
Quarterly30 minExport all data, check free-plan limits, review AI privacy, update links and prices
Annually60 minReview tools, insurance, licenses, tax questions, and whether the business still fits you

Put these on the calendar with the same seriousness as a client meeting. The business is also a client.

The low-energy version

Some weeks you will have 15 minutes and a flat battery. Do this instead of skipping entirely:

  • Tiny week: open the tool, do one transaction, write one next action, or send one follow-up.
  • Admin-only week: download one export and put it in the backup folder.
  • No-buy week: cancel one unused subscription or decline one upsell.
  • Ask-for-help week: send one short email to the SBDC, SCORE, or a mentor.
  • Rest week: read one chapter and write one question. That counts.

ADHD-friendly, low-energy productivity is not a moral failure. It is a design requirement. Smaller sessions are allowed.

If you only do three things

  1. Separate the money and keep a monthly money date.
  2. Put a one-page website and a way to contact you online.
  3. Book free human help before you pay for advice.

Everything else can wait until a real limit appears.

A printable session checklist

THIS WEEK'S SESSION

[ ] Set a 45-minute timer
[ ] Open only the tools for this session
[ ] Do the real task, not the tutorial
[ ] Export or save the result

The freebie scorecard

Before you build a habit around a free tool, score it on these ten points. Any "no" is a conversation with yourself, not automatically a dealbreaker.

  1. Real free tier: Can you do the core job forever, or is this a short trial?
  2. Core-job completeness: Does the free plan require a paid add-on for the thing you actually need?
  3. Export: Can you get your data out in a usable format? Have you tested it?
  4. Limits: Do you know the contact, document, storage, send, or usage caps?
  5. Commercial use: Does the licence allow business use, client work, or resale? Check the actual licence.
  6. Privacy and data use: What does the provider collect, and does it train on your data? Is the tool appropriate for the information you're putting in it?
  7. Security: Two-factor authentication, access controls, and a credible security page.
  8. Support: Can you get help without paying, and is there a real documentation page?
  9. Longevity: Is the provider established, and do you have a replacement plan if the free tier changes?
  10. Total cost: Domain, payment processing, storage, exports, upsells, and your time. "Free" is not the same as "no cost."

The exit test: Before you store anything important, find the export button, export a sample, and open the file. If you cannot leave, do not move in.

Scam and trap patterns

Free tools and government programs attract copycats. These patterns are common:

  • "Free government grant" calls or texts. SBA does not call you out of the blue to award a grant. Grants are specific, competitive, and documented on official sites. Never pay a fee to "release" a grant.
  • Paid EIN or LLC filing services. You can apply for an EIN free at the IRS and file formation documents at INBiz. Third-party services can be legitimate, but cold calls and look-alike sites are not the place to start.
  • Look-alike government domains. A site with an SBA logo and a slightly wrong URL is not the SBA. Type sba.gov, irs.gov, inbiz.in.gov, or in.gov yourself.
  • Free trials with automatic renewal. Put a cancellation reminder on your calendar before the trial ends. Use a virtual card or a payment method with a low limit if available.
  • "Lifetime" deals with no export. A lifetime price on a tool that holds your only copy of customer data is a hostage situation, not a bargain.
  • Fake mentors and guaranteed approvals. A legitimate free advisor does not demand payment, gift cards, crypto, or your bank login. Verify the organization through the SBDC, SCORE, or SBA.
  • "Free" templates you cannot use commercially. Read the licence. Personal-use-only templates are not a business foundation.
  • AI tools that ask for credentials. Never paste passwords, API keys, or recovery codes into a chat. A legitimate AI product does not need them to draft an email.
  • Unsolicited tax or bookkeeping help. Verify the preparer's credentials and the official filing channel. A confident stranger is not a CPA.

Report fraud: https://reportfraud.ftc.gov/ and https://www.ic3.gov/. Report suspected impersonation to the agency being imitated.

How to re-check a freebie in 10 minutes

Once a quarter, for each tool you depend on:

  1. Open the official pricing page and note today's date.
  2. Check the limits against your current usage.
  3. Read the data-use and training settings.
  4. Test an export and open the file.
  5. Check whether the plan still covers the core job.
  6. Look for a replacement that can import your data.
  7. Update your own notes—not just this guide.

If you adapt this guide for your audience, keep the checked date visible and re-verify the links before you publish. A confidently outdated freebie list is worse than no list.

What this guide does not cover

  • Payroll, benefits, and multi-state employment.
  • Inventory, manufacturing, and complex e-commerce operations.
  • Insurance selection, loan underwriting, and grant applications.
  • International tax, privacy, and business formation.
  • Regulated industries, including healthcare compliance beyond the education-only guardrails here.
  • Securities, investments, and financial advice.
  • Any guarantee about free-plan longevity, tool quality, or eligibility.

For those, use the official agency and a licensed professional. Free tools are infrastructure; they are not professional judgment.
